question: When a reservoir computer forecasts chaotic dynamics, does jointly tuning a deliberate training-noise amplitude produce a nonzero optimum for both short trajectories and long-run attractor behavior?

key_findings.claim: A nonzero input-noise amplitude is selected when noise is optimized jointly with the reservoir's five other hyperparameters.
key_findings.evidence: Bayesian surrogate optimization selects amplitudes 10^-3.42 and 10^-1.97 for Mackey-Glass delays 17 and 30, and 10^-2.35 for the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system, alongside spectral radius, input scale, leakage, ridge penalty, and connection probability.

key_findings.claim: Short-horizon accuracy, stability, and valid prediction time show a fitted interior optimum in the two displayed chaotic systems.
key_findings.evidence: For every fixed noise amplitude from 10^-8 to 10^-0.5, the other five hyperparameters are reoptimized. Across 80 performing reservoirs, Figure 3 displays U-shaped RMSE and bell-shaped stability and horizon curves for Mackey-Glass at delay 30 and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, with optima near the jointly selected noise levels.

key_findings.claim: The same noise region improves the paper's long-run attractor-deviation score, but the evidence is based on selected projections rather than a full invariant-measure test.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 reports minima of a deviation value for Mackey-Glass and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky at noise amplitudes consistent with the short-term optima. The visual audit shows that the score is computed in two-dimensional coordinates—delay embedding for Mackey-Glass and two spatial values for Kuramoto-Sivashinsky—so unshown modes and temporal statistics can still differ.

key_findings.claim: The optimal-noise result is conditional on a large, noise-specific hyperparameter search rather than an isolated causal effect of noise.
key_findings.evidence: Each point in the noise sweep receives a fresh optimization of spectral radius, input scaling, leakage, regularization, and connectivity. This is a fair best-case comparison for each amplitude, but it does not show whether noise is still beneficial under equal search budgets, a fixed reservoir, or standard default tuning.

key_findings.claim: The proposed stochastic-resonance mechanism remains speculative.
key_findings.evidence: The paper argues that useful noise should be of the same order as noiseless one-step error and suggests noise-enhanced generalized synchronization, but it gives no state-space synchronization measurement, causal intervention on that mechanism, or theory that predicts the optimum.

key_findings.claim: The main PDF is not self-contained enough to reproduce the strongest claim.
key_findings.evidence: Reservoir equations, the RMSE and deviation-value definitions, per-noise hyperparameter tables, robustness variants, reservoir-size results, and synchronization discussion are deferred to supplementary information that is referenced but not included in the indexed seven-page manuscript.

method.core_idea: Treat deliberate input-noise amplitude as a model hyperparameter and look for an interior optimum after retuning the rest of the reservoir for every noise level.
method.mechanism: Add Gaussian noise to the normalized training series; use surrogate-based Bayesian optimization over noise, spectral radius, input scale, leakage, ridge penalty, and reservoir connectivity; then evaluate autonomous rollouts through RMSE, thresholded stability, valid horizon, and a projected attractor-deviation score.
assumptions: The selected reservoir and readout can represent the Mackey-Glass and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics.
Synthetic Gaussian input noise resembles the perturbations for which robustness is needed.
Every noise level receives a comparable and sufficiently converged hyperparameter search.
The chosen RMSE thresholds and two-dimensional attractor projections preserve the model ordering of interest.
Training and test trajectories are stationary and lie in the same dynamical regime.

techniques.role: Makes augmentation strength a jointly optimized coordinate instead of a fixed nuisance.
Uses a fixed random recurrent state map with a fitted readout for autonomous chaotic forecasting.
Interpolates expensive hyperparameter trials with radial basis functions to propose new candidates.
Measures how long prediction error remains below a chosen threshold.
Compares projected long-run trajectories when pointwise chaotic forecasts have necessarily diverged.

evaluations.setting: Mackey-Glass delay equation at delays 17 and 30, with 150,000 normalized training steps.
evaluations.metric: RMSE, stability probability, prediction horizon, and projected-attractor deviation.
evaluations.result: The selected nonzero noise improves the displayed short and long prediction measures; delay 30 uses noise amplitude 10^-1.97.
evaluations.baseline: Reservoirs at lower and higher fixed noise amplitudes, including effectively noiseless training, with the other five hyperparameters reoptimized.

evaluations.setting: Kuramoto-Sivashinsky PDE on domain length 60 with seven positive Lyapunov exponents and about 1,000 Lyapunov times of training data.
evaluations.metric: Five-to-six-Lyapunov-time field error, 100-Lyapunov-time projected attractor, stability, horizon, and deviation value.
evaluations.result: The displayed curves have an interior optimum around noise amplitude 10^-2.35 and the selected rollout visually follows the reference field and projected attractor.
evaluations.baseline: The same reservoir family across a logarithmic noise sweep with separate hyperparameter optimization.

limitations: Author-stated: no tractable double-well-style theory explains the resonance in the high-dimensional reservoir.
Author-stated: generalized synchronization is proposed only as a plausible mechanism.
Reviewer inference: only two synthetic system families and one reservoir-computing pipeline are tested.
Reviewer inference: a separate five-dimensional hyperparameter search at every noise level makes compute and optimizer variance part of the treatment.
Reviewer inference: Figure 3 uses only the subset termed performing reservoirs, and the selection rule is not stated in the main manuscript.
Reviewer inference: projected attractor proximity can miss wrong invariant density, modes, correlations, Lyapunov exponents, and rare events.
Reviewer inference: the indexed main paper omits the supplement containing core definitions and robustness details.
failure_modes: Noise smooths away weak but dynamically important high-frequency structure.
The apparent interior optimum comes from uneven hyperparameter-search convergence or postselection.
A two-dimensional projection matches while the full attractor or invariant measure is wrong.
The useful synthetic-noise level fails when deployment noise has different scale, spectrum, correlation, or missingness.
The RMSE threshold changes which amplitude maximizes stability or horizon.
A fixed compute budget makes per-amplitude Bayesian retuning impractical.
reusable_insights: Augmentation strength should be tuned jointly with model dynamics, not appended after tuning the noiseless model.
Chaotic forecasting needs separate short-horizon, rollout-stability, and invariant-statistics metrics.
An interior regularization optimum is not by itself evidence for a named physical mechanism.
When every treatment receives retuning, report search cost, failures, and optimizer uncertainty as part of the comparison.
Projected attractor plots should be paired with joint-distribution, temporal-correlation, spectral, and rare-event diagnostics.
open_questions: Does the optimal amplitude remain nonzero under equal total tuning compute and preregistered noise grids?
Can generalized synchronization measurements predict the optimum before the expensive sweep?
How does useful training noise depend on observation noise, model error, sample interval, Lyapunov spectrum, and reservoir width?
Does the effect transfer to neural operators, state-space models, transformers, and partially observed physical systems?
Which full-distribution metric best validates the long-run climate without privileging a selected projection?
Can correlated, colored, adversarial, or state-dependent noise outperform isotropic Gaussian injection?

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic Approach for Assessing the Predictability of Chaotic Time Series Using Reservoir Computing
competitive_landscape.difference: Khovanov treats numerical and observational uncertainty as stochastic structure in training data and uses it to audit reservoir predictability. The reviewed work instead deliberately injects and tunes noise as a performance intervention and claims an interior resonance.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Dissipative Dynamics in Chaotic Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: Li and colleagues stabilize long operator rollouts with synthetic off-attractor contraction and Sobolev losses, then evaluate many invariant statistics. The reviewed paper regularizes with input noise and searches its amplitude, but supplies no boundedness mechanism or comparable full statistical panel.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3 and NeurIPS 2022 record checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Reservoir Computing with Noise
competitive_landscape.difference: Nathe and colleagues separate training and testing noise and find best performance when their strengths match, with low-pass filtering as a remedy. That deployment-noise interaction is absent from the reviewed clean-test resonance and can explain why one universal training amplitude should not be expected.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalized Teacher Forcing for Learning Chaotic Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Hess and colleagues modify teacher forcing to prove all-time bounded gradients and reconstruct attractor geometry with tractable recurrent models. The reviewed approach uses an unproved noise mechanism and fixed random reservoirs, targeting prediction robustness rather than gradient stability and low-dimensional reconstruction.

competitive_landscape.title: DySLIM: Dynamics Stable Learning by Invariant Measure for Chaotic Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: DySLIM directly regularizes a model toward the estimated invariant measure and reports pointwise plus statistical accuracy. The reviewed method obtains robustness indirectly through noise and validates long-run behavior with a narrower projection-based deviation score.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Jointly optimized training noise induces a stochastic resonance that dramatically improves short-term and attractor prediction in reservoir computers.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Two chaotic system families display fitted interior optima across error, stability, horizon, and a projected attractor-deviation score after other reservoir hyperparameters are separately optimized at each noise level.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The useful empirical contribution is the controlled noise sweep with per-level retuning and multiple short/long rollout scores. Calling it stochastic resonance is descriptive rather than mechanistic: the generalized-synchronization explanation is untested, the core supplement is absent, and search variance or deployment-noise matching are live alternatives. Later work directly studies train/test noise, bounded gradients, dissipativity, and invariant-measure objectives, so a current follow-up should preregister equal-compute searches and full-distribution validation.

reviewer_notes: Read all seven indexed pages and rendered Figures 1-4 and Table I at full resolution. The curve panels visibly support an interior optimum but also show broad ensemble scatter and fitted smoothing. The manuscript delegates essential equations, deviation-score details, hyperparameter tables, robustness variants, and mechanism analysis to a separate supplement not contained in the indexed PDF; claims depending on those items were therefore kept conditional. Primary arXiv, OpenReview, ICML, NeurIPS, and PMLR records were checked through 2026-08-23.
